docs.title: Self-Hosting Guide
docs.text:
BibMedEd runs as a set of Docker containers. You need Docker (with Compose) and Git.

Never used Docker? Install Docker Desktop for your OS (Mac/Windows/Linux — free for academic and non-commercial use). After installing, open Docker Desktop once so it can start its background service, then proceed with the Quick Start below. The whole BibMedEd stack runs locally inside the containers — no cloud account, no external services. Git can be installed from git-scm.com.

Want to look around before installing anything? Read the end-to-end case study — it walks through a real research question with screenshots and a sample methodology log so you can decide if BibMedEd fits your workflow before committing to the install.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/ata381/BibMedEd
cd BibMedEd/bibmeded
docker compose up

After the containers finish starting (usually 30-60 seconds the first time), open http://localhost:3000 — that's BibMedEd. The interactive API docs are at http://localhost:8000/docs.

This starts five services:

Service Port Description Frontend localhost:3000 Next.js web interface API localhost:8000 FastAPI backend Worker — Celery task processor PostgreSQL localhost:5432 Database Redis localhost:6379 Message broker + cache

The database schema is created automatically on first startup.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text:
BibMedEd has no built-in authentication

BibMedEd is designed as a single-tenant, self-hosted tool for one research team — there is no login, no user accounts, and no per-project access control anywhere in the API. Every endpoint (list projects, run searches, read or export publications, bulk-exclude records, delete a project) trusts the numeric ID in the URL with no notion of an "owner." That's a reasonable tradeoff for a tool that runs on localhost or inside a lab's private network, but it means anyone who can reach the API has full read/write access to every project — including via the one-click "Deploy to Cloud" button, which provisions a publicly reachable *.onrender.com URL by default with no credentials required.

Before exposing BibMedEd to the public internet, do one of the following:

  • Keep it private (recommended) — run it on localhost or inside a VPN/private network, which is the default docker compose up setup. Don't forward ports 3000/8000 to the public internet.
  • Restrict by IP — Render's Inbound IP Rules (Scale/Enterprise plans) let you allowlist your lab's IP range for the bibmeded-api and bibmeded-frontend web services so only your team can reach them.
  • Put an auth proxy in front — add HTTP basic auth with a reverse proxy such as Caddy's basicauth directive or nginx's auth_basic, so every request needs a shared password before it reaches BibMedEd.

Treat an unprotected BibMedEd deployment the same way you'd treat an admin panel with no login screen — because that's exactly what it is.

docs.title: Public read-only demo
docs.text:
Setting BIBMEDED_READ_ONLY=true turns an instance into a public demo that visitors can explore without installing anything, and that they cannot change.

When the flag is on:

  • Every non-GET/HEAD/OPTIONS request is rejected with 403 and {"detail": "...read-only public demo...", "read_only": true}. This is enforced by a middleware that runs before routing, so it also covers endpoints added in future releases and paths that don't exist. WebSocket connections are closed with code 1008. Blocked today: creating, renaming, or deleting projects; creating the sample project; triggering searches; bulk or single exclusion; and running analyses.
  • No outbound API calls can be triggered. Searches (PubMed, OpenAlex, CrossRef, Semantic Scholar, Lens.org) and iCite enrichment only ever run inside a Celery task dispatched by POST /search, which is blocked. A read-only deploy therefore needs no Redis and no worker, and /api/ready reports "redis": "skipped".
  • The database refuses writes from requests, as a second line of defence. Request sessions use a separate engine whose connections the database itself holds read-only: Postgres connections start with default_transaction_read_only=on (merged with any ?options= already in BIBMEDED_DATABASE_URL), and SQLite connections run PRAGMA query_only = ON. The setting is re-applied every time a connection is taken from the pool, and startup fails unless a probe (SHOW transaction_read_only = on, or PRAGMA query_only = 1) confirms the guard is active. Any write path (ORM flush, Core insert/update/delete, Query.update, raw SQL, bulk helpers) fails; ORM flushes are reported as 403, other paths as a logged 500. Other database backends are refused outright. The startup seeder uses the normal, writable engine. GET /search/{query_id} still reports a stale running search as failed, but no longer persists that change.
  • The bundled sample project is seeded on startup (if missing), and all six analyses are precomputed so the dashboard has data even though POST /analysis/{type} is blocked. Seeding is idempotent and fails the startup loudly if the database is unreachable.
  • All exports keep working (CSV, RIS, Web of Science plain text, JSON, PRISMA SVG, methodology log, bundle zip) because they are GET downloads.
  • GET /api/config returns {"read_only": true}; the web UI uses it to show a "Read-only demo" banner and hide or disable create, delete, search, exclusion and analysis-run controls. If the endpoint can't be reached, the UI assumes read-only.
  • Startup logs BibMedEd mode: read_only=<true|false> and warns about any BIBMEDED_* environment variable that matches no setting (for example BIBMEDED_READONLY).

docs.title: Run the demo locally
docs.text:
One command, no Postgres, Redis or worker:

cd bibmeded
docker compose -f docker-compose.demo.yml up --build

Open http://localhost:3100 (API docs at http://localhost:8100/docs). The API seeds the bundled synthetic sample into a disposable SQLite file inside the container on every start. The ports differ from the main docker-compose.yml, so both stacks can run side by side. Stop and discard everything with docker compose -f docker-compose.demo.yml down -v.

docs.title: Host a free public demo on Render
docs.text:
deploy/render-demo.yaml is a separate Blueprint (the root render.yaml is for self-hosting and does not create demo services). It defines two free web services and no database, Redis or worker.

  1. In the Render dashboard choose New → Blueprint, select your fork of the repository, and set Blueprint Path to deploy/render-demo.yaml.
  2. Apply it. If Render gives the services URLs other than https://bibmeded-demo-api.onrender.com and https://bibmeded-demo-frontend.onrender.com (a taken name gets a suffix), edit the two literal URLs in the file (BIBMEDED_CORS_ORIGINS and NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL) and redeploy. The API URL is baked into the frontend at build time, so changing it needs a rebuild.
  3. Run the smoke check from the deploy checklist below.

Free web services sleep when idle, so the first visit after a quiet period waits roughly a minute for a cold start, and the demo data is rebuilt each time. The data is the bundled synthetic sample, not real research data. SQLite needs no SELECT-only role because the file is disposable and rebuilt on boot.

Deploy checklist

  1. Smoke-check every deploy: curl -fsS https://<demo-api>/api/config must print {"read_only":true}, and curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -X POST https://<demo-api>/api/projects must print 403. Fail the deploy otherwise.
  2. Optionally deny non-GET/HEAD/OPTIONS methods at the proxy too, so a misconfigured app is still protected. For example, in nginx: limit_except GET HEAD OPTIONS { deny all; }; in Caddy: @write not method GET HEAD OPTIONS followed by respond @write 403.
  3. Add a per-IP rate limit at the proxy (see below).

Run the demo against its own database — never point a read-only instance at a database that holds real projects, since every project in it becomes publicly readable.

Residual risks

Read-only mode stops mutation and outbound calls; it does not make a public instance hardened.

  • Denial of service. Every read still hits the database, and /export/bundle builds a zip in memory. Put a reverse proxy or CDN in front with a per-IP rate limit (for example nginx limit_req zone=bibmeded burst=20 at around 5 requests/second, or Caddy's rate_limit, or Cloudflare rate-limiting rules), plus request-size and timeout limits.
  • No rate limiting in BibMedEd itself. The application does not throttle clients; that has to happen at the proxy.
  • Everything in the database is public. Only seed demo data.
  • Interactive API docs remain available at /docs. "Try it out" on a write endpoint just returns 403, but you can hide the docs at the proxy if you prefer.
  • Configuration mistakes. The flag defaults to false; if the environment variable is missing the instance is fully writable. A misspelled BIBMEDED_* name is logged as a warning at startup, but the deploy smoke check above is the real safeguard.
  • The database guard can be lifted by SQL that asks for it. A statement such as SET TRANSACTION READ WRITE or PRAGMA query_only = OFF would undo the guard for its connection until that connection goes back to the pool, when it is re-applied. BibMedEd never issues one, and no endpoint accepts SQL, but for a stronger boundary give the demo API a database role with only SELECT privileges (seed with a separate writable role first).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Copy .env.example to .env to customize:

cp .env.example .env
Variable Default Description BIBMEDED_PUBMED_API_KEY (empty) Optional. Register free at NCBI. With a key, PubMed requests run at 10 req/s; without one, at 3 req/s BIBMEDED_NCBI_EMAIL (empty) Optional contact email sent to NCBI on every PubMed search/fetch request. Requests identify the tool as bibmeded; blank email and API-key values are omitted. BIBMEDED_PUBMED_RATE_LIMIT (empty) Optional. PubMed requests per second. Empty means 10 with a key and 3 without. A value here must be a positive finite number, always wins and is not capped, so stay within NCBI's limits BIBMEDED_OPENALEX_EMAIL (empty) Optional. Sent to OpenAlex as mailto= BIBMEDED_CROSSREF_EMAIL (empty) Optional. Sent to CrossRef as mailto= BIBMEDED_SEMANTIC_SCHOLAR_API_KEY (empty) Optional. Semantic Scholar keyed tier (1 req/s sustained) BIBMEDED_LENS_API_KEY (empty) Required only for Lens.org searches. Scholarly API bearer token BIBMEDED_READ_ONLY false Public demo mode — see Public read-only demo POSTGRES_USER bibmeded Database username POSTGRES_PASSWORD bibmeded Database password POSTGRES_DB bibmeded Database name

All defaults work out of the box — no .env file is required. docker-compose.yml passes the BIBMEDED_* source settings above into both the api and worker containers; BIBMEDED_READ_ONLY goes to the api only. The PubMed rate a search used is recorded in its methodology step and printed in the methodology export as "Request rate limit".

docs.title: Stopping
docs.text: docker compose down

docs.title: Resetting the Database
docs.text:
To wipe all data and start fresh:

docker compose down -v
docker compose up

The -v flag removes the PostgreSQL data volume.

docs.title: Development Setup
docs.text:
For contributors, the docker-compose.override.yml file automatically enables:

  • Hot-reload on Python file changes
  • Source code volume mounts

To disable dev mode (e.g., for local production testing), rename or remove the override file:

mv docker-compose.override.yml docker-compose.override.yml.bak
docker compose up --build

docs.title: Health Check
docs.text:
Verify the API is running:

curl http://localhost:8000/api/health
# {"status": "ok"}

docs.title: Liveness and readiness probes
docs.text:
For Docker / Kubernetes / Render and any orchestrator that needs a deep healthcheck, BibMedEd exposes two split probes:

  • GET /api/live — liveness. Returns {"status": "alive"} with no I/O. Suitable for the docker-compose healthcheck.test on the api service and the Kubernetes livenessProbe. Never fails as long as the process is up.
  • GET /api/ready — readiness. Pings Postgres (SELECT 1) and Redis (PING). Returns 200 {"status":"ready","checks":{"db":"ok","redis":"ok"}} when both are reachable, 503 {"status":"not_ready","checks":{...}} otherwise. Use as the Kubernetes readinessProbe or the load balancer healthcheck.

Example docker-compose snippet:

services:
  api:
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-fsS", "http://localhost:8000/api/live"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3

Every API response includes an X-Request-ID header (auto-generated unless the client supplies one). When filing a bug, include this id so logs can be correlated end-to-end.

docs.title: Scripting BibMedEd
docs.text: BibMedEd is primarily a self-hosted web app, but every UI action is also a REST endpoint. This page is for researchers who want to drive the tool from a Jupyter notebook, batch over many topic queries, or pull deduplicated data into a pandas / polars pipeline.

docs.title: List available sources from the CLI
docs.text:
Inspect registered bibliographic adapters and whether their API keys are configured:

bibmeded sources
bibmeded sources --json

Each JSON entry reports api_key_requirement as required, optional, or no; key values are never printed:

{"name": "lens", "display_name": "Lens.org", "api_key_requirement": "required", "status": "missing BIBMEDED_LENS_API_KEY"}

docs.title: Install from PyPI (CLI only)
docs.text:
If you only want the command line tool (no Docker, no web UI), install it with pipx install bibmeded or into a dedicated virtual environment (recommended, to keep its dependencies isolated):

python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate   # Python 3.12 or newer
pip install bibmeded
bibmeded search "medical education" --source openalex --dry-run

The base install is lightweight and supports --dry-run result estimates. Fetching and storing records (bibmeded search without --dry-run) goes through the Celery pipeline, so it additionally needs the server extra plus Redis and a database, or simply the Docker stack:

pip install "bibmeded[server]"

docs.title: Estimate search results from the CLI
docs.text:
Before fetching a large result set, use --dry-run to estimate how many records a query will return:

bibmeded search "machine learning" --dry-run

docs.title: OpenAPI surface
docs.text:
When the API is running locally:

  • Interactive Swagger UI: http://localhost:8000/docs
  • ReDoc: http://localhost:8000/redoc
  • Raw OpenAPI 3.1 spec: http://localhost:8000/openapi.json

Use the raw spec with openapi-generator to generate a typed client in Python, TypeScript, R, or any other supported language.

docs.title: Versioning contract
docs.text: Every analysis response carries a schema_version field. As of v0.2.0 the version is "1.0". Additive changes (new optional keys on existing endpoints) do not bump the version; breaking changes do. Pin against this field in any downstream pipeline you build.

docs.title: Minimal Python example (httpx)
docs.text:
No code generation needed for simple scripting — the raw API is small enough:

import httpx

API = "http://localhost:8000"
with httpx.Client(base_url=API, timeout=60) as c:
    # 1. Create a project
    project = c.post("/api/projects", json={"name": "AI in MedEd 2024"}).json()
    pid = project["id"]

    # 2. Trigger a search
    c.post(f"/api/projects/{pid}/search", json={
        "query_string": '(Artificial Intelligence[Mesh]) AND (Education, Medical[Mesh])',
        "source": "pubmed",
        "year_start": "2020",
        "year_end": "2024",
        "max_results": 2000,
    })

    # 3. Poll until completed
    import time
    while True:
        status = c.get(f"/api/projects/{pid}/search/latest").json()
        if status["status"] in {"completed", "failed"}:
            break
        time.sleep(2)

    # 4. Run an analysis
    authors = c.post(f"/api/projects/{pid}/analysis/authors").json()
    print(authors["results"]["schema_version"])  # "1.0"
    print(authors["results"]["top_authors"][:5])

    # 5. Pull the deduplicated dataset as versioned JSON
    payload = c.get(f"/api/projects/{pid}/export/json").json()
    print(f"{payload['count']} publications, schema_version={payload['schema_version']}")

docs.title: Bulk export for downstream ML
docs.text:
The /api/projects/{id}/export/json endpoint returns a single JSON object with a stable publication schema (pmid, doi, title, abstract, year, authors, keywords, citation_count, excluded, exclusion_reason, etc.). For pandas:

import pandas as pd
import httpx

resp = httpx.get(f"http://localhost:8000/api/projects/{pid}/export/json")
payload = resp.json()
df = pd.json_normalize(payload["publications"])
df.to_parquet("corpus.parquet")

For the full submission bundle (CSV + RIS + Web of Science plain text + JSON + methodology + PRISMA SVG + screening decision log CSV + manifest in one .zip), hit /api/projects/{id}/export/bundle.

docs.title: Web of Science plain text for VOSviewer and Bibliometrix
docs.text:
GET /api/projects/{id}/export/wos returns the included records in the Web of Science tagged plain-text format (.txt, UTF-8 with a byte-order mark, as Clarivate writes it). This is the format VOSviewer reads under Create map → Read data from bibliographic database files → Web of Science, and the one Bibliometrix reads with:

library(bibliometrix)
M <- convert2df("project-wos-2026-10-12.txt", dbsource = "wos", format = "plaintext")

The file opens with FN Clarivate Analytics Web of Science and VR 1.0. Each record starts with PT J and ends with ER and a blank line, and the file ends with EF. A field with several values (authors, addresses, cited references) puts one value per line, with continuation lines indented by three spaces. A field BibMedEd has no value for is left out, never written empty. Line breaks inside values are replaced by spaces, so a value cannot start a new tag or record.

Tag Content Source in BibMedEd PT Publication type, always J constant AU One author per line, Surname, Initials author name AF One author per line, Surname, Given names author name TI Title title SO Source title journal name DT Document type publication type, as the source gave it DE Author keywords, separated by ; keywords the source supplied (not MeSH) ID MeSH terms, separated by ; MeSH terms AB Abstract abstract C1 One address per line, [Authors] Affiliation, Country. author affiliations (see below) CR One cited reference per line, SURNAME I, YEAR, SOURCE, DOI <doi> or DOI <doi> reference list (see below) NR Number of references the source reported reference list TC Times cited citation count SN, EI ISSN, eISSN journal PY Publication year year DI DOI DOI UT Unique record id, <SOURCE>:<id> such as PUBMED:31234567 or OPENALEX:W2741809807 source and source-native id PM PubMed ID, PubMed records only PMID

Known gaps:

  • Cited references. BibMedEd stores each record's references as identifiers, not as the Author, Year, Source, Volume, Page, DOI strings Web of Science writes. A reference that resolves to a record in the same export, by DOI or by source-native id (an OpenAlex ID, a Lens ID, a PMID) using the same matching as the citation analysis, is written in WoS cited-reference form from that record: first-author surname and initials, year and journal name, all upper case, then the DOI, for example DEMIR SA, 2019, MEDICAL EDUCATION, DOI 10.1111/medu.13900. Parts the cited record lacks are left out. Any other reference that is a DOI is written as bare DOI <doi>, because BibMedEd holds nothing else about it. References that are neither are left out of CR; NR still gives the full count, and the bundle's MANIFEST.txt states how many of the references reached CR. PubMed does not return reference lists, so PubMed records have no CR or NR.
  • What this means in each tool. Bibliometrix's local-citation analysis (histNetwork, localCitations) matches a CR entry against each record's first author, year and source plus its DOI, so it counts citations between records of the same export and nothing else; a bare DOI <doi> never matches. VOSviewer's co-citation maps of cited sources and cited authors read the source and author out of each CR entry, so they are only populated by the full-form, in-corpus references; bare DOI <doi> entries contribute neither. Both tools see a citation network limited to the exported corpus.
  • Author names. PubMed names arrive as Surname, Given; a PubMed author without a comma is a collective author and is written unchanged. Other sources give Given Surname, and the last word is taken as the surname. Surnames with particles (van der Berg) and organisation names from those sources are split at the last word too.
  • Addresses. Affiliations belong to an author record, not to a paper, and author records are shared across the whole database by normalised name (all projects, all sources). C1 therefore lists every affiliation BibMedEd holds for that name, which can include affiliations seen on other papers, or on another person with the same normalised name. Each address is the stored affiliation text; when the text does not already end with the stored country (aliases such as England for UK count as ending with it), the country is appended, because VOSviewer takes the last comma-separated part as the country. Every address ends with a period, because Bibliometrix splits addresses and matches countries on it.
  • ID holds MeSH terms, not Clarivate's KeyWords Plus, and UT is not a Web of Science accession number. Bibliometrix reads both as plain text, so analyses run, but results labelled "Keywords Plus" are MeSH-based.
  • Not exported: language, volume, issue, pages, funding, reprint address, research areas and cited-reference details, because BibMedEd does not store them.

docs.title: CSV export columns
docs.text:
The CSV export contains these columns in order:

Column Meaning PMID PubMed identifier, when available DOI DOI, when available Title Publication title Authors Authors separated by ; Journal Journal name Year Publication year Citations Recorded citation count; empty when no count is available, while 0 means a recorded zero Keywords Keywords separated by ; Abstract Abstract text, with line breaks flattened to spaces

The empty Citations cell intentionally preserves the difference between missing data and a measured zero; downstream Excel, R, and pandas workflows should not coerce it to 0.

docs.title: Batch over many queries
docs.text:
Searches are dispatched to Celery and return HTTP 202 immediately. To batch 50 queries:

import asyncio, httpx

async def run_one(c, topic):
    project = (await c.post("/api/projects", json={"name": topic})).json()
    await c.post(f"/api/projects/{project['id']}/search", json={
        "query_string": topic, "source": "pubmed", "max_results": 500,
    })
    return project["id"]

async def main(topics):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(base_url="http://localhost:8000", timeout=60) as c:
        return await asyncio.gather(*[run_one(c, t) for t in topics])

Polling cadence is up to you. The status endpoint at GET /api/projects/{id}/search/latest is cheap.

docs.title: Rate limits and politeness
docs.text:
Upstream APIs (PubMed E-utilities, OpenAlex, CrossRef, Semantic Scholar, Lens.org) have their own rate limits. BibMedEd respects each adapter's documented courtesy patterns (mailto= for OpenAlex / CrossRef, api_key for PubMed, Semantic Scholar, and Lens.org). Set these in bibmeded/.env before starting the worker:

BIBMEDED_PUBMED_API_KEY=...
BIBMEDED_NCBI_EMAIL=you@example.com
BIBMEDED_OPENALEX_EMAIL=you@example.com
BIBMEDED_CROSSREF_EMAIL=you@example.com
BIBMEDED_SEMANTIC_SCHOLAR_API_KEY=...
BIBMEDED_LENS_API_KEY=...

docker compose up passes these into the api and worker containers. PubMed requests run at 10 per second when BIBMEDED_PUBMED_API_KEY is set and 3 per second otherwise; BIBMEDED_PUBMED_RATE_LIMIT overrides both. The rate used is recorded in the search step of the methodology log.

The Celery soft time limit is 600 seconds per task — for very large windowed searches you may want to split by year range and merge.

docs.title: Author productivity (Lotka's law)
docs.text:
The authors analysis ranks authors by the h-index (Hirsch 2005), g-index (Egghe 2006) and e-index (Zhang 2009), all computed within the project's corpus. Its lotka block fits Lotka's law (Lotka 1926): the number of authors with n papers is about C / n^alpha, with alpha close to 2 in many fields.

  • distribution lists every productivity level (papers, authors). Authors are counted in full on every included paper they co-wrote (complete counting), so the levels sum to total_authors.
  • fit.alpha and fit.C come from a least-squares line through log10(authors) against log10(papers), over every level with no tail cutoff. fit.r_squared is the R² of that line. A few single authors with many papers carry as much weight as the many authors with one paper and pull alpha towards 1, so read alpha together with the distribution.
  • fit.goodness_of_fit is the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of Pao (1985). It compares the observed cumulative share of authors with the Lotka distribution for the fitted alpha. That distribution has C = 1 / zeta(alpha) (expected_single_paper_share), so the test needs alpha > 1. consistent_with_lotka is true when D is below the 0.01-level critical value 1.63 / sqrt(N). That formula holds only for more than 35 authors, so smaller corpora get D without a verdict.
  • With fewer than 3 distinct productivity levels, or the same number of authors at every level, fit is null and reason says why. Two points always fit a line exactly, so an exponent from them would mean nothing.

The methodology export recomputes the fit from the included records and logs the method, its parameters, the distribution and the result, or the reason no fit was made, under "AUTHOR PRODUCTIVITY (Lotka's law)". The distribution line is enough to recompute alpha, C, R² and D from the log alone. The lotka block is an additive field, so schema_version stays "1.0".

docs.title: Methodology export from scripts
docs.text: GET /api/projects/{id}/export/methodology returns the citable PRISMA-aligned text log. GET /api/projects/{id}/export/prisma returns the SVG. Both reflect manual exclusions made through the toggle / bulk-exclude endpoints, so a fully programmatic workflow can still produce a journal-quality methodology section.

docs.title: Screening decision log
docs.text:
Every exclude, re-include and bulk-exclude appends one row per changed record to an append-only screening decision log, in the same transaction as the change. A row holds the UTC time, the endpoint (toggle or bulk_exclude, with the citation threshold for bulk exclusions), the record's exclusion state, reason and stage before and after, and an optional reviewer label. The bundled sample project logs its one seeded exclusion with source sample_seed and no reviewer. BibMedEd has no accounts, so the label is whatever the client sends in the X-Reviewer header. Use ASCII letters, digits, spaces and . _ @ ' ( ) -, start with a letter or digit, and keep it to 64 characters at most. Anything else is rejected with 422. Without the header no reviewer is recorded, and none is invented.

c.patch(f"/api/projects/{pid}/publications/{pub_id}/exclude",
        json={"reason": "wrong_population"}, headers={"X-Reviewer": "Reviewer A"})

The methodology log has a "Screening decision history" section. It gives the number of decisions (exclusions, reversals where an excluded record is re-included, and reason or stage changes), the first and last decision times, exclusion decisions by stage and reason, every bulk-exclude request, and the reviewer labels seen. Each bulk-exclude request gets a run_id (a UUID) that is stored on every decision row it writes. It also gets a bulk_exclude methodology step with the run id, the threshold and the matched, excluded and skipped counts. A request that matches nothing therefore still shows up in the export. These steps cover the whole project. They are listed in this section and are not counted in the pipeline totals or the PRISMA diagram. The export bundle adds <project>-screening-decisions-<date>.csv with one row per decision, including its run_id. The log starts at Alembic revision 0006_screening_decisions and is not backfilled, so the section also counts excluded records that have no logged decision. Downgrading that revision refuses to drop logged decisions unless BIBMEDED_ALLOW_LOSSY_DOWNGRADE=1 is set.

docs.title: Screening stages
docs.text:
PRISMA 2020 reports screening in two stages: title/abstract screening of records and full-text assessment of reports. Every exclusion carries a screening_stage:

Value PRISMA 2020 box title_abstract Records excluded (beside "Records screened") full_text Reports excluded, or Reports not retrieved when the reason is fulltext_unavailable

Both exclude endpoints accept an optional screening_stage. When it is omitted or null:

  • reason fulltext_unavailable is recorded at full_text, because PRISMA 2020 counts a report that could not be retrieved under "Reports not retrieved", a full-text box;
  • every other reason is recorded at title_abstract, so clients written before stages existed keep their old meaning.

Sending fulltext_unavailable with an explicit "screening_stage": "title_abstract" is a contradiction and returns 422 whenever the request would exclude. The API rejects it rather than silently changing the stage.

# Exclude a record at full-text assessment
c.patch(f"/api/projects/{pid}/publications/{pub_id}/exclude",
        json={"reason": "wrong_outcome", "screening_stage": "full_text"})
# -> {"id": ..., "excluded": true, "exclusion_reason": "wrong_outcome", "screening_stage": "full_text"}

# Bulk-exclude low-citation records (stage defaults to title_abstract)
c.post(f"/api/projects/{pid}/publications/bulk-exclude", json={"citation_threshold": 0})
# -> {"excluded_count": ..., "reason": "other", "screening_stage": "title_abstract"}

The endpoint is a toggle: calling it on an excluded record re-includes it and clears both exclusion_reason and screening_stage, whatever the body says (a re-include is never refused for the contradiction above). A record has one stage, the stage it was excluded at; to move an exclusion to the other stage, re-include it and exclude it again. GET /api/projects/{id}/publications returns screening_stage on every publication (null while it is included). The data exports (CSV, RIS, Web of Science, JSON) contain only included records, so stages appear in exports through the methodology log and the PRISMA diagram counts.

The flow diagram counts reports sought for retrieval as records screened minus title/abstract exclusions, and reports assessed for eligibility as reports sought minus reports not retrieved. The methodology log lists both stages with per-reason counts.

Alembic revision 0004_screening_stage backfills exclusions that existed before stages: fulltext_unavailable exclusions become full_text (so they appear under "Reports not retrieved"), and every other exclusion becomes title_abstract. If any excluded record still has no stage, both exports count it by the same rule (fulltext_unavailable under "Reports not retrieved", anything else at title/abstract) and say how many there are. Downgrading the revision refuses to run while full-text exclusions exist, because it would erase their stage. Export the methodology log first, then set BIBMEDED_ALLOW_LOSSY_DOWNGRADE=1 to proceed.

These are additive response fields, so schema_version stays "1.0".

docs.title: Troubleshooting and FAQ
docs.text:
This page collects the problems people run into most often, with the message you will see and what to do about it. It is written for researchers, not developers. You do not need to read any code.

Most fixes need a terminal open in the bibmeded/ folder of your BibMedEd download, the folder that holds docker-compose.yml. Every docker compose command below is run from there.

If your problem is not here, see Where do I report a bug? at the end.

docs.title: docker compose up says it cannot connect to Docker
docs.text:
Cannot connect to the Docker daemon at unix:///var/run/docker.sock. Is the docker daemon running?

On Windows the same problem usually mentions dockerDesktopLinuxEngine and ends with The system cannot find the file specified.

Docker is installed but its background service is not running. Open Docker Desktop, wait until it reports that the engine is running, then run docker compose up again. Docker Desktop has to be open whenever you use BibMedEd. See the Self-Hosting Guide if you have not installed Docker yet.

docs.title: A port is already in use (3000, 8000, 5432 or 6379)
docs.text:
Docker's wording varies by system, but it names the port, for example:

Bind for 0.0.0.0:5432 failed: port is already allocated

BibMedEd publishes four ports on your computer: 3000 (web app), 8000 (API), 5432 (PostgreSQL) and 6379 (Redis). Another program, or a second copy of BibMedEd, is already using one of them.

  1. Find the program using the port. On Windows: netstat -ano | findstr :5432. On macOS or Linux: lsof -i :5432.
  2. If it is an old BibMedEd stack, stop it with docker compose down.
  3. If it is another program, such as a PostgreSQL you installed yourself, stop that program while you use BibMedEd.

If you cannot stop a local PostgreSQL or Redis, you can move BibMedEd's copy instead. In docker-compose.yml, change only the number on the left of the colon, for example "5432:5432" to "5433:5432". The BibMedEd containers talk to the database and Redis inside Docker, so nothing else needs to change.

docker-compose.yml is part of the downloaded code, so a later git pull refuses to run while your edit is in it. Before updating, run git stash to set the edit aside, then git pull, then git stash pop to put it back. Moving the port in docker-compose.override.yml does not avoid this: that file is also part of the download, and Docker Compose adds ports listed there to the original ones instead of replacing them.

Ports 3000 and 8000 are harder to move: the web app has the API address (NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL) built in, and the API only accepts requests from the web app's address (BIBMEDED_CORS_ORIGINS). Free those two ports rather than changing them.

docs.title: The api or worker container exits with "no such file or directory" (Windows)
docs.text:
no such file or directory

If this mentions scripts/entrypoint.sh, the start-up script was checked out with Windows line endings. Linux containers cannot run it that way. The repository now forces Unix line endings for shell scripts, but a copy cloned before that fix keeps the old file.

Clone the repository again into a new folder, then rebuild:

git clone https://github.com/ata381/BibMedEd
cd BibMedEd/bibmeded
docker compose up --build

--build matters: without it Docker reuses the image that contains the broken file.

docs.title: Does it run on an Apple Silicon Mac (M1 and later)?
docs.text:
Nothing in BibMedEd is specific to Intel or ARM. The compose files do not pin a CPU platform, and every image is built from an official base image (postgres:16-alpine, redis:7-alpine, python:3.12-slim, node:20-alpine) that is published for both. Plain docker compose up is all you need, with no extra flags.

BibMedEd's automated tests do not run on ARM. If a build fails on a Mac, please report it with the full output.

docs.title: I started the demo and it is on port 3100, not 3000
docs.text:
That is intended. The read-only demo (docker compose -f docker-compose.demo.yml up --build) uses http://localhost:3100 for the web app and http://localhost:8100/docs for the API, so it can run next to your normal BibMedEd on 3000 and 8000. It has no database server, no Redis and no worker. It shows only the bundled synthetic sample and does not let you create projects or run searches. See Run the demo locally.

Stop it and discard its data with:

docker compose -f docker-compose.demo.yml down -v

docs.title: How do I start over with an empty database?
docs.text:
This deletes every project:

docker compose down -v
docker compose up

-v removes the PostgreSQL data volume. See Resetting the Database. Contributors can also run docker compose exec api python scripts/reset_db.py, which drops and recreates every table. That script is meant for development only.

docs.title: PubMed searches fail with "429 Too Many Requests"
docs.text:
In the web app the search stops and you see:

Search failed. Please try again.

The worker log (docker compose logs worker) shows the reason:

run_search failed query_id=12
...
httpx.HTTPStatusError: Client error '429 Too Many Requests' for url 'https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?...'

NCBI limits how many requests one computer may send to PubMed: 3 per second without an API key and 10 per second with one. BibMedEd paces each search at 3 requests per second. The worker runs up to two searches at the same time, so two PubMed searches together, or other PubMed tools on the same network, can go over the keyless limit.

Fix:

  1. Create a free API key in your NCBI account settings.
  2. Copy .env.example to .env in the bibmeded/ folder if you have not already, and set BIBMEDED_PUBMED_API_KEY=your_key.
  3. Restart so the containers pick it up: docker compose down, then docker compose up.
  4. Run the search again.

The key raises NCBI's limit for you. BibMedEd still sends at most 3 requests per second per search, so it does not search faster. It does stop two searches at once from going over the limit. Without a key, run one PubMed search at a time.

docs.title: Lens.org searches fail: "Lens searches require BIBMEDED_LENS_API_KEY"
docs.text:
Lens.org is the only built-in source that needs a key. Without one, BibMedEd refuses the search before contacting Lens. The API answers with status 503:

{"detail": "Lens searches require BIBMEDED_LENS_API_KEY"}

The web app only shows a general message:

Could not start search. Is the backend running?

The command line prints Lens searches require BIBMEDED_LENS_API_KEY, and bibmeded sources lists Lens as missing BIBMEDED_LENS_API_KEY.

Fix: get a Scholarly API token from Lens.org, add BIBMEDED_LENS_API_KEY=your_token to bibmeded/.env, then run docker compose down and docker compose up. The Lens chip on the search page is marked "(API key)" as a reminder.

docs.title: My search finished with 0 results, but the query is correct
docs.text:
The search page shows 0 publications ready. and the results page says "No publications found". Check these in order:

  1. Publication years. The Query Builder starts at 2022 to 2025. Widen the range if your topic is older.
  2. PubMed syntax sent to another database. Field tags such as [Mesh], [tiab] and [PDAT] only work in PubMed. OpenAlex and Lens.org take plain keywords combined with AND, OR and NOT. Remove the tags, or switch the source to PubMed.

CrossRef and Semantic Scholar are a different case: they run a free-text relevance search and do not apply AND, OR and NOT as Boolean logic. With them, the usual problem is the opposite of zero results: a broad set of loosely related records that fills the 2,000-record cap. For a precise Boolean strategy, use PubMed, OpenAlex or Lens.org. 3. Advanced Query (Raw) mode. For PubMed, the year range is part of the query text: it is the [PDAT] clause the Query Builder adds. In raw mode, type it yourself. For the other sources, the year fields are hidden in raw mode, but the years you last set in the Query Builder are still applied. Switch back to the Query Builder to check them. 4. Test the count without fetching anything. From the command line, bibmeded search "your query" --source openalex --dry-run prints Estimated results: N. The dry run ignores year limits, so a large number here and 0 in the app points to the years.

docs.title: Did my search hit the 2,000-record cap?
docs.text:
Each search fetches at most 2,000 records by default, so one broad query cannot run for hours. For PubMed searches with a cap below 10,000, BibMedEd tells you when the database had more. The results page shows:

Search returned 5,400 records — only the first 2,000 were fetched.

and the methodology log records:

    Results: 5400 records (capped at max_results=2000; full set not retrieved)

The warning is not reliable for other sources or at 10,000

For OpenAlex, CrossRef, Semantic Scholar and Lens.org, and for PubMed with the cap at 10,000, a truncated search currently shows no warning, and the methodology log does not mark it as capped (#151). Until that is fixed, treat any search whose Records identified number equals the cap exactly (2,000, or the cap you set) as truncated. Check the real total with bibmeded search "your query" --source openalex --dry-run, which prints Estimated results: N. The dry run ignores year limits, so narrow the query until the count is below the cap.

For a systematic review you need the full set. Either:

  • Narrow the query (fewer years, more specific terms) until it returns fewer than 2,000 records, or run it in parts, for example one search per range of years. Searches in the same project are deduplicated against each other.
  • Raise the cap, up to 10,000. The web app always asks for 2,000. Use the API page at http://localhost:8000/docs: open POST /api/projects/{project_id}/search, choose Try it out, and send "max_results": 10000 with your query. See Scripting for a script that does the same. The API rejects values above 10,000. A search has 10 minutes to finish (the worker's time limit), so very large searches can also fail. Splitting by year avoids both limits.

For very large searches, the "Records identified" number can be lower than the database's full total, because BibMedEd stops collecting IDs once it has enough. --dry-run gives the full count.

docs.title: My search stays on "Search dispatched..." and never progresses
docs.text:
Searches run in the separate worker container. If the worker is not running, the search waits in the queue with status pending and nothing moves. The command line shows the same thing:

Status: pending
Status: pending
...
Search timed out. Check worker logs

Check the containers:

docker compose ps
docker compose logs worker

If worker is missing or has exited, start it with docker compose up -d worker. Searches waiting in the Redis queue are picked up when the worker starts. If a search is still pending after that, for example because Redis was restarted in the meantime, run it again. If the worker log shows an error, include it in a bug report.

A search that has been running for more than 15 minutes is reported as failed, so it does not appear stuck forever. Run it again once the worker is healthy.

docs.title: Why are two records with the same title both kept?
docs.text:
BibMedEd only treats two records as duplicates when they share the same DOI or the same PMID, exactly. It never compares titles. Titles are not unique: corrections, conference abstracts and preprints often repeat a title word for word, and merging those automatically would hide real records from your PRISMA counts. DOIs are compared without letter case and without a leading https://doi.org/, http://doi.org/ or doi:.

So two records with the same title are both kept when:

  • one has a DOI and the other does not, or they have different DOIs, and
  • they do not share a PMID.

Records with neither a DOI nor a PMID can never be matched. If you find a duplicate yourself, exclude one copy on the results page with the reason Duplicate (missed by automated dedup). The methodology log counts it as "Duplicate not caught by automated dedup".

docs.title: Which wins, DOI or PMID?
docs.text:
Either one is enough. A record is a duplicate if its DOI or its PMID matches a record already seen, and the first copy is kept. When both match, the methodology log counts the removal under doi, otherwise under pmid.

Within one project, BibMedEd also checks every new record against the records already saved, by PMID (or the source's own ID) and DOI. A paper that an earlier search already found is usually not saved twice, and the copy saved first is kept. There is one known gap (#153): if a paper first arrives from OpenAlex (or another non-PubMed source) and a later PubMed search returns it without a DOI, the two are not matched and both are kept. Exclude the extra copy as a duplicate.

docs.title: Where do I find how many duplicates were removed?
docs.text:
There are two places:

  • The results page: the "Duplicates removed" box in the PRISMA flow, for the latest search.
  • The methodology log (Export page, Methodology & PRISMA), in the DEDUPLICATION section of each search:
DEDUPLICATION
  Step 3: Cross-source deduplication on DOI and PMID
    Method: exact-match on doi,pmid
    Removed by field: doi=4, pmid=1
    Removed: 5 duplicates (412 → 407)

This section only appears when a search removed at least one duplicate. BibMedEd fetches records in batches of 200 and this count covers duplicates inside a batch. Two kinds of skipped records are not listed here: records an earlier search in the same project already had, and duplicates that fall in different batches of the same search. Both count as unavailable in that search's DATA COLLECTION step:

    Retrieved: 380 of 400 (20 unavailable)

The "unavailable" count also includes records the database listed but did not return, and records that failed to save. Failed records are listed one by one under Failed to persist.

docs.title: Which screening stage does an exclusion get?
docs.text:
PRISMA 2020 separates title/abstract screening of records from full-text assessment of reports. Each exclusion records one of the two:

  • In the web app, the exclusion menu has a PRISMA screening stage choice, Title / abstract or Full text. It starts at Title / abstract on each visit and stays on your last choice while you work. Full-text not retrievable is always recorded at the full-text stage, because PRISMA reports it as "Reports not retrieved".
  • Exclude 0-citation papers records its exclusions at title/abstract with the reason "Other / unspecified".
  • Through the API, the stage is optional. When you leave it out, fulltext_unavailable goes to full_text and every other reason goes to title_abstract. Details are in Screening stages.

docs.title: "Exclude 0-citation papers" wants to exclude almost everything
docs.text:
Citation counts come from NIH iCite, and BibMedEd only fetches them for PubMed searches. Records from OpenAlex, CrossRef, Semantic Scholar and Lens.org have no citation count. The bulk exclusion counts "no citation count" as 0, so it would remove every one of them. The confirmation dialog shows how many publications will be excluded. Read that number before confirming.

If a PubMed search's records all show 0 citations, check the methodology log for iCite citation count enrichment (failed). iCite was unreachable during that search. The search itself still succeeded.

The methodology log records how many records were excluded and why, not the threshold you used. State the threshold in your Methods section.

docs.title: The API returns 422 when I exclude with fulltext_unavailable
docs.text:
Value error, reason 'fulltext_unavailable' records a report that could not be retrieved, which PRISMA 2020 counts at the full-text stage; use screening_stage 'full_text' or omit it

You asked for reason fulltext_unavailable at stage title_abstract. Those two contradict each other, and BibMedEd refuses rather than quietly changing the stage. Send "screening_stage": "full_text", or leave the stage out. The web app never sends this combination, so you only see this from scripts.

docs.title: How do I re-include a record, or move it to the other stage?
docs.text: On the results page, click Excluded on the record. It goes back to included and its reason and stage are cleared. Through the API, calling the exclude endpoint again on an excluded record does the same. A record has only one stage. To move an exclusion to the other stage, re-include it, then exclude it again at the stage you want.

docs.title: The dashboard does not change after I exclude records or run another search
docs.text:
The first time you open the dashboard, BibMedEd calculates the six analyses and stores the results. Later visits show those stored results. Nothing recalculates them after you exclude records or run a new search (#152), so the dashboard can describe an older version of your corpus. This also affects the answers below.

Until that is fixed, recalculate by hand:

  1. Note your project's number. It is in the address bar: http://localhost:3000/projects/7/dashboard is project 7.
  2. Open http://localhost:8000/docs and find POST /api/projects/{project_id}/analysis/{analysis_type}.
  3. Choose Try it out, enter the project number, and run it once for each of publications, authors, countries, keywords, citations and journals.
  4. Reload the dashboard.

Do this again after every round of exclusions or new searches, and before you export figures or numbers for a paper.

docs.title: The dashboard says "No publications to analyze"
docs.text: The dashboard counts included records that have a publication year. This message means there were none when the analyses were stored. Either no search had finished, every record was excluded, or no record has a year. Check the included count on the results page. If you have included records with years now, the dashboard is showing old stored results: recalculate them.

docs.title: The growth summary shows "—" instead of CAGR or doubling time
docs.text:
The publication trends figure shows compound annual growth (CAGR) and doubling time, measured over full calendar years only. When one cannot be calculated, the card says why:

Message Meaning At least two full calendar years of data are required to compute CAGR. The included records span fewer than two complete years. CAGR is undefined because the first full calendar year has zero publications. Growth from zero cannot be expressed as a rate. Start the search at a later year. Doubling time is not defined for non-positive growth (CAGR <= 0). Output is flat or shrinking, so it never doubles. CAGR is still shown. Current incomplete year excluded from growth calculations. Not an error. The current year is still in progress, so it is left out.

If the message no longer matches your corpus, the dashboard is showing old stored results. Recalculate them.

docs.title: Field maturity is null or "undetermined"
docs.text:
The field maturity classification is not shown on the dashboard. It is in the publications analysis returned by the API (field_maturity in GET /api/projects/{id}/analysis/publications). That request returns 404 with Analysis not found. Run it first. until the analysis has been calculated once, by opening the dashboard or with POST on the same address. The GET returns the stored result, so recalculate after changing the corpus.

The classification fits a logistic growth curve to cumulative publication counts:

  • null: the first and last publication years span fewer than four calendar years, counting both ends (for example 2021 to 2023 is three), or the curve could not be fitted.
  • "phase": "undetermined": a curve was fitted but explains the data poorly (fit quality below 0.85). BibMedEd does not guess a phase label in that case. Plateau-then-surge fields often end up here.

docs.title: The network says "No network data available", or a table is empty
docs.text:
The dashboard network is the co-authorship network. It is empty when no included record lists its authors, or when the stored analysis predates your search (recalculate). Large networks (more than 200 authors) start by showing only about the 100 most productive authors. Lower the Min. publications slider to see more.

Other analyses depend on what each source provides:

  • Countries are read from the end of author affiliation text and match a fixed list of about 50 countries. Semantic Scholar gives no affiliations, so a Semantic Scholar-only project has no country or institution data. OpenAlex records store only the institution name, such as "Harvard University", without a country, so OpenAlex-only projects have almost no country data (#154).
  • Citation counts are only filled for PubMed searches (see above). Other sources show 0 citations, and author h-indices will be 0.
  • MeSH terms come from PubMed and Lens.org. For the other sources, keyword analyses use only the keywords that source supplies.

docs.title: Which file do I open in which program?
docs.text:
Export Opens in Notes RIS (.ris) Zotero, EndNote, Mendeley Title, authors, journal, year, DOI, abstract and keywords. CSV (.csv) Excel, Google Sheets, R, pandas One row per record: PMID, DOI, title, authors, journal, year, citations, keywords and abstract. Cells that start with =, +, - or @ get a leading ' so the spreadsheet does not treat them as formulas. JSON (.json) Scripts and notebooks A schema_version field (currently "1.0"), the project name, the date, a count and the publications. Check schema_version before relying on field names. See Scripting. Methodology log (.txt) Any text editor The record of every pipeline step. See below. PRISMA diagram (.svg) Web browser, Word, PowerPoint, Inkscape The PRISMA 2020 flow diagram with your counts. Bundle (.zip) Your file manager All five files above plus a manifest.

CSV, RIS and JSON contain included records only. The methodology log and the PRISMA diagram give the number of excluded records per stage and reason, but do not list which records they were. To keep a list of your exclusions, export the CSV before you exclude anything and again afterwards, and compare the two.

docs.title: Where does the methodology log go in my paper?
docs.text:
The log is a plain-text record of what BibMedEd did. It lists, for each search, the exact query, the database, the date and time it ran, how many records were found and retrieved, any cap that was hit, duplicates removed by field, and citation enrichment. After the searches it lists screening decisions by PRISMA stage and reason, then the final number of included studies.

A common pattern:

  • In Methods, report the databases, the exact queries and search dates, and the deduplication rule (exact match on DOI and PMID). Copy these from the log rather than retyping them.
  • Attach the full log as a supplementary file and refer to it from Methods.
  • Use the PRISMA SVG as your flow diagram figure.
  • Cite BibMedEd itself. The case study has an example sentence, and the citation is on the home page.

docs.title: Every change fails with 403 "read-only public demo"
docs.text:
{"detail": "This BibMedEd instance is a read-only public demo. Install BibMedEd locally to create projects and run your own searches.", "read_only": true}

The instance runs with BIBMEDED_READ_ONLY=true. That setting blocks every request that would change something: creating or deleting projects, searching, excluding and running analyses. Exports still work. This is deliberate for public demos. See Public read-only demo.

On your own install, check bibmeded/.env and your environment for BIBMEDED_READ_ONLY=true. Set it to false, then run docker compose down and docker compose up. The API log prints BibMedEd mode: read_only=False at start-up when writes are allowed.

docs.title: My own install shows the "Read-only demo" banner
docs.text:
Read-only demo — install locally to run your own searches.

If BIBMEDED_READ_ONLY is not set to true, the web app could not reach the API to ask, and it stays read-only to be safe. The search button then does nothing. Usually the API is still starting or has stopped. Check with:

docker compose ps
curl http://localhost:8000/api/config

When the API answers {"read_only":false}, reload the page.

If the API answers correctly but the banner stays, check the address in your browser. The API only accepts the web app at exactly http://localhost:3000. Opening it as http://127.0.0.1:3000, or from another computer through a network address, makes the configuration request fail, and the app stays read-only. Open exactly http://localhost:3000.

docs.title: A misspelled setting is being ignored
docs.text:
If you run BibMedEd without Docker, or on Render, the API log warns at start-up about any BIBMEDED_ variable it does not recognise:

ignoring unrecognised environment variable BIBMEDED_READONLY (typo of a BIBMEDED_* setting?)

With docker compose there is no warning. Docker Compose only passes a fixed list of variables from bibmeded/.env into the containers (see docker-compose.yml), so a misspelled name never reaches the API and is silently ignored. Several correctly spelled settings are not passed either (#148). Compare your .env with bibmeded/.env.example and the configuration table, fix the spelling, and restart.

docs.title: Can I put my BibMedEd on the internet?
docs.text: Not as it is. BibMedEd has no login: anyone who can reach it can read, change or delete every project. Keep it on your own computer or a private network, or put an IP allowlist or a password-protecting proxy in front. Read the Security model first.

docs.title: How do I upgrade to a new version?
docs.text:
git pull
docker compose up --build

When the containers start, they update the database structure automatically with alembic upgrade head. The log shows Running Alembic migrations... before the API starts. Your projects are kept. Let running searches finish before you upgrade.

The web app's packages are kept in a separate Docker volume that is filled only the first time. If the web app fails to start or shows errors after an update (check docker compose logs frontend), remove that volume so it is rebuilt from the new version:

docker compose down
docker volume rm bibmeded_frontend_node_modules
docker compose up --build

Do not use docker compose down -v for this

-v removes every volume, including the database. All your projects would be deleted.

If you run BibMedEd without Docker, run alembic upgrade head from the bibmeded/ folder after updating.

docs.title: A downgrade refuses to run because of full-text exclusions
docs.text:
Going back to a version from before screening stages existed would delete the stage of every full-text exclusion. Those exclusions would then read as title/abstract exclusions. The downgrade stops with:

0004_screening_stage downgrade: 3 publication(s) were excluded at the full-text stage, and dropping publications.screening_stage would erase that stage (they would read as title/abstract exclusions after re-upgrading). Export the methodology log and PRISMA diagram for every affected project first, then re-run with BIBMEDED_ALLOW_LOSSY_DOWNGRADE=1 to accept the loss. Refusing to silently drop reproducibility-critical screening data.

First export the methodology log and PRISMA diagram for every affected project. Then, with the current version still checked out, run the downgrade with the setting given to that one command only:

docker compose run --rm -e BIBMEDED_ALLOW_LOSSY_DOWNGRADE=1 api alembic downgrade 0003_sample_project_key

Run the downgrade before you switch to the older code. An older release does not know the newer database revision, so starting it on an upgraded database fails with an Alembic Can't locate revision error instead.

docs.title: Where do I report a bug?
docs.text:
Open an issue on GitHub with the bug report template. It asks for:

  • what happened, how to reproduce it, and what you expected;
  • your version: bibmeded --version, or docker compose exec api bibmeded --version if you use Docker, plus git rev-parse --short HEAD if you run from a clone;
  • how you run BibMedEd (local Docker Compose, Render, or other);
  • the output of docker compose logs api worker around the failure.

If the API answered with an internal error (status 500), the response body contains a request_id:

{"detail": "Internal server error", "request_id": "3f9c2a1b7d4e"}

Include it so the matching log lines can be found. Every other response carries the same id in its X-Request-ID header.

Other routes:

  • Questions and ideas: GitHub Discussions.
  • A new data source: the adapter request template.
  • A feature request: the feature request template.
  • Security problems: do not open a public issue. Follow SECURITY.md to report privately.

docs.title: BibMedEd 0.4: install from PyPI, a redesigned interface, and a read-only demo mode
docs.text: BibMedEd 0.4.0, released on 2026-09-30, is the first version published to PyPI. It also brings a redesigned frontend, a read-only mode for showing a seeded project safely, and two CLI commands from first-time contributors. One change is breaking: the Python import package was renamed from app to bibmeded.

docs.title: Install the CLI from PyPI
docs.text:
pip install bibmeded now installs a lightweight command-line tool, with no Docker and no web UI (#84):

python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate   # Python 3.12 or newer
pip install bibmeded

bibmeded --version
bibmeded sources
bibmeded search "medical education" --source openalex --dry-run

The base install covers --version, sources and search --dry-run. Fetching and storing records still runs through the Celery pipeline, so a full bibmeded search needs the server extra (pip install "bibmeded[server]") plus Redis and a database, or the Docker stack. See Scripting & API.

Two of these commands are community contributions:

  • bibmeded --version prints the installed version (#72, by @Sandro850).
  • bibmeded sources lists the registered adapters and whether each one's API key is configured; add --json for machine-readable output (#71, by @DYNOSuprovo). Key values are never printed.

docs.title: Breaking: the import package is now bibmeded
docs.text:
The Python package was renamed from app to bibmeded, so the wheel no longer installs a generic top-level app package (#97). If you run BibMedEd outside the provided Docker Compose files, update your commands:

uvicorn bibmeded.main:app
celery -A bibmeded.workers.celery_app worker

Celery task names are now bibmeded.workers.tasks.*. Drain queued tasks before you upgrade, because tasks queued under the old names will not be picked up.

docs.title: A redesigned interface
docs.text: The frontend has a new journal-editorial look, and the redesign includes WCAG 2.2 accessibility fixes (#75). The screenshots on the home page show the new interface with the bundled sample corpus.

docs.title: Show a project without letting anyone change it
docs.text:
Setting BIBMEDED_READ_ONLY=true rejects every mutating request with 403 and shows a read-only banner in the UI (#81). Visitors can browse a seeded project, its analyses and its exports, but cannot create, delete, search or exclude.

You can try this mode locally with one command, with no Postgres, Redis or worker (#86):

cd bibmeded
docker compose -f docker-compose.demo.yml up --build

Then open http://localhost:3100. The same release ships a free-plan Render Blueprint, deploy/render-demo.yaml, for hosting your own demo. The project does not run a hosted public demo yet; that is deliberately deferred. Read Public read-only demo before exposing an instance, since everything in a read-only instance's database is publicly readable.

docs.title: Fresh installs work on SQLAlchemy 2.1
docs.text: SQLAlchemy 2.1 changed the default driver for bare postgresql:// URLs to psycopg v3, so fresh installs failed with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'psycopg'. BIBMEDED_DATABASE_URL values of postgres:// or postgresql:// are now normalised to postgresql+psycopg2:// (#76). URLs that name a driver, and non-Postgres URLs, are left as they are.

docs.title: Try it or help shape it
docs.text:
• Follow the quick start and choose Explore sample project.
  • Read the end-to-end case study.
  • Share a real workflow or question in GitHub Discussions.
  • Claim a focused task from the good first contributions list.

The full list of changes in 0.4.0, and in every earlier release, is in the CHANGELOG.

BibMedEd remains a single-tenant, self-hosted tool without built-in authentication. Do not expose a writable deployment directly to the public internet; review the security model first.

docs.title: Why BibMedEd?
docs.text: The short version: bibliometric reviews in medical education currently require four tools — search, screening, analysis, visualisation — and a fifth (Excel) to glue them together. BibMedEd does all of them in one self-hostable application and writes your PRISMA methodology section as it goes.

docs.title: Who this page is for
docs.text: You arrived here because you were searching for something like "Covidence alternative", "free VOSviewer replacement", "open-source bibliometric tool", or "how do I run a systematic review without Excel". This page is a fair-handed comparison so you can pick the right tool — sometimes that's not BibMedEd.

docs.title: The capability matrix
docs.text:

Legend: ✅ first-class · ⚠️ partial · 📋 on roadmap · ❌ not supported.

docs.title: Pick BibMedEd if you want
docs.text:
• One integrated app from search → analysis → export.
  • A PRISMA methodology log generated automatically rather than reconstructed at write-up time.
  • To self-host on a lab server or a researcher's laptop without per-seat fees.
  • To plug in a new bibliographic source (institutional repository, niche database) without negotiating with a vendor.
  • A modern web UI usable by non-programmer collaborators in your research group.

docs.title: Pick Covidence if you want
docs.text:
• A dual-reviewer screening workflow with conflict resolution and inter-rater reliability metrics — this is Covidence's main strength and BibMedEd hasn't shipped it yet (roadmap item).
  • Institutional support contracts and training.
  • You can absorb the per-seat or per-review pricing.

docs.title: Pick VOSviewer if you want
docs.text:
• A polished, battle-tested desktop tool for network visualisation specifically.
  • You already have a deduplicated .ris or .csv and only need the network.
  • Reproducible static images for a publication figure (VOSviewer's rendering is excellent).

docs.title: Pick CiteSpace if you want
docs.text:
• Burst detection, dual-map overlay, and timeline visualisations — CiteSpace's signature features.
  • Decades of methodological literature behind specific analyses.

docs.title: Pick Bibliometrix if you want
docs.text:
• A mature R-native workflow you can pipe through dplyr / ggplot2 / quarto.
  • The biblioshiny GUI for a no-code experience inside RStudio.
  • A vast literature of published methods using the package — peer reviewers will recognise it.

docs.title: Pick pyBibX if you want
docs.text:
• Python-native programmatic analysis with built-in LLM-based topic interpretation.
  • Notebook-driven workflows where the analysis lives next to your data wrangling.

docs.title: Where BibMedEd is honestly weaker today
docs.text:
• Single-reviewer screening only. Dual-reviewer with conflict resolution is on the roadmap but Covidence ships it today.
  • Frontend visualisations are interactive but not publication-ready. VOSviewer and CiteSpace produce better static images for journal figures; BibMedEd exports the underlying data so you can re-render in either if needed.
  • Adapter coverage is still growing. PubMed, OpenAlex, CrossRef, Semantic Scholar, and Lens.org ship; Europe PMC, arXiv, DOAJ, OpenCitations, CORE, and BASE are open issues waiting on contributors (adapter label). Scopus and Web of Science require paid API agreements.
  • No published bibliometric methodology paper yet — a JOSS-style paper.md is maintained in the repository, and submission is planned once there is independent research use. Nothing has been submitted yet. Bibliometrix's methodology paper has thousands of citations; we have zero so far.

We'd rather be honest about these gaps than oversell. If any of them are dealbreakers, pick a tool above and come back when the gap closes (or — better — open the PR that closes it).

docs.title: Where BibMedEd is structurally better
docs.text:
• The methodology log is novel. No other tool on this list emits a citable text record of every pipeline step — search query, source, retrieval timestamp, dedup decisions, exclusion filters, analysis runs — that you paste straight into your PRISMA 2020 Methods section. This isn't a feature you can bolt onto the others.
  • The adapter pattern is the entire extensibility story. Every other tool above either accepts a fixed set of import formats or is single-source. BibMedEd ships five adapters (PubMed, OpenAlex, CrossRef, Semantic Scholar, Lens.org) at ~50-250 lines each; more are open issues with claim-it labels, and the registry auto-discovers any new BaseSourceAdapter dropped into bibmeded/adapters/ — no registration step.
  • Cross-source deduplication is automatic, not "import then dedupe in Excel." DOI and PMID matching happens at retrieval time and is logged.
  • Web-native, multi-user-ready architecture. VOSviewer and CiteSpace are desktop tools; Bibliometrix is R-bound; pyBibX is a Python library. BibMedEd is a FastAPI service designed to run on a lab server with shared access — a deployment shape none of the alternatives offer.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/ata381/BibMedEd
cd BibMedEd/bibmeded
docker compose up

Open http://localhost:3000. Or click the Render deploy button on the README for a zero-install cloud spin-up.
